question.prompt:
The graph of the function \(f\) is shown below. How many solutions does the equation \(f(f(x)) = 6\) have?

[Figure 1](figures/2002_AMC_12A_Q19_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Work backward from the outer function. If \(t=f(x)\), then we need \(f(t)=6\). The graph reaches height \(6\) only at the two labeled peaks, whose inputs are \(-2\) and \(1\). Therefore
\[
f(f(x))=6
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(x)=-2\ \text{or}\ f(x)=1.
\]

[Figure 1](figures/2002_AMC_12A_Q19_question_fig1.svg)

Now count intersections with these two horizontal levels. The line \(y=-2\) crosses each outer segment once. It misses both middle segments, whose heights run from \(0\) to \(6\). This gives two solutions.

The line \(y=1\) crosses all four segments once, giving four more solutions. Each segment rises or falls strictly, so it contributes at most one intersection at either level. Neither level passes through a joining vertex, so no intersection has been counted twice.

All six inputs lie in the displayed domain \([-7,5]\). Their outputs, \(-2\) or \(1\), also lie in that domain, so the second evaluation of \(f\) is defined. An input cannot have both outputs, so the two groups are disjoint. The total is \(2+4=\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Read the graph twice
Read successive preimages from the graph
Solve on the four line segments
